name: Undershot waterwheel
note: Rome already operates these at scale. The water pushes on the bucket; it is simple, portable, and tolerates muddy water and sand.

name: Overshot waterwheel
note: Rome has this too, notably the 16-wheel Barbegal complex. Weight of the water does the work; it needs a significant drop but delivers more power per wheel.

name: Treadwheel crane
note: Roman construction cranes driven by human walk inside the wheel. The mechanical advantage is immediate and the load is obvious to the worker.

name: Animal-driven treadmill
note: Ox or horse walks inside a large wheel to power mill machinery or pumps. Available wherever you have animals; used at Roman mines.

name: Sails on ships
note: Rome uses wind to move ships. This is free power once mastered; the wind will not supply electricity or mechanical work directly ashore without new capture technology.

name: Force pump
note: Roman force pumps lift water by mechanical displacement, not by suction alone. Critical for aqueducts and mines; requires a slave or animal to operate.

name: Screw press
note: The screw and nut multiply force: oil, wine, coins. Rome has perfect screw threads; this is a force multiplier, not power generation.

name: Horizontal waterwheel (Norse)
note: The rotor spins on a vertical axis, driven by a direct vertical jet. No complex gearing needed, no right-angle transmission. Rugged, efficient for small streams with drop.

name: Breastshot waterwheel
note: Water hits the wheel at mid-height, between overshot and undershot. Smeaton measured efficiency systematically: breastshot wins by combining gravity and impulse when head is moderate. This is how empirical engineering began.

name: Efficiency measurement of waterwheels
note: Smeaton built test wheels and measured their output vs input with weights and pulleys, not guessing. This is the birth of hydraulic engineering as a science: quantitative, reproducible, publishable.

name: Millpond and storage
note: A dam and reservoir upstream of the mill, holding water during low flow, releasing it when needed. This gives you power when the stream does not: seasonal agriculture, milling, mining.

name: Leat and weir
note: The leat is a conduit bringing water from higher up the valley, often in an aqueduct on stonework or timber. The weir diverts water from the river. Together they concentrate flow and head at the mill site.

name: Peat extraction and burning
note: Bog digging gives you fuel where forest is scarce. Peat burns slower and wetter than wood but is abundant in northern Europe. Not Rome's world yet, but available in the North.

name: Oil shale and bitumen deposits
note: Oil shale and bitumen seeps exist; heating shale gives a bituminous liquid. The yield is poor and transport is heavy, but it is available without drilling if you find the deposits.

name: Water turbine (Fourneyron)
note: The turbine runner spins fast, with fixed guide vanes and moving buckets, using the entire head at any flow. This beats a wheel because it accelerates the water to high speed and extracts the momentum, not just the weight. The penalty: it needs better tolerances and materials.

name: Pelton wheel
note: A jet of water hits a double-cup bucket at high speed, splitting the jet tangentially to the wheel. Ideal for very high heads with low flow. The bucket profile is critical; casting is easier than machining but requires controlled cooling to avoid cracks.

name: Hydroelectric power station
note: A dam, penstock, turbine, and dynamo coupled: water flow becomes rotary motion becomes electrical current. The scale is decided by head and flow. Long-distance transmission at high voltage makes remote hydro economical.

name: Post mill
note: The entire mill building pivots on a post to face the wind. It is portable, fits anywhere, and gives you wind power without a tall fixed tower. The miller rotates it by hand or rope from a tail pole.

name: Tower mill
note: A fixed tapered brick or stone tower with a rotating cap. Taller and heavier than a post mill, it catches stronger winds and is more stable. The rotary bearing is now high stress, needing good metalwork.

name: Windmill fantail and automatic furling
note: A small perpendicular fan on the tail of the cap automatically rotates the mill to face the wind. If the wind is too strong, the fan spins faster, which tilts a striker linkage that furls the sail. No miller attendance needed at night.

name: Trompe (water-driven air blast)
note: Falling water entrains air in a angled tube, compressing it as the water drops. The compressed air separates from the water at the bottom, no valves, no moving parts. Ingenious; useful for furnace blast in a mine or forge where you cannot afford bellows labour.

name: Tide mill
note: A mill at the estuary with gates that open on incoming tide, close on outgoing, releasing a head of water. Twice per 24 hours, not continuous, but free and predictable. Requires careful site and sluice design.

name: Coal seam and mining
note: Coal is buried stone that burns: anthracite in deep seams. Mining requires shoring and drainage. Early mines are shallow; deep coal demands ventilation and pumping to stay safe and dry.

name: Coking: coal to coke
note: Heating coal without air produces coke (carbon) and coal tar. Coke is almost pure carbon: hotter burning, less ash and sulfur than coal. Essential for iron smelting at scale in a blast furnace.

name: Coal gas and gasworks
note: Heating coal in a retort produces flammable gases: hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide. These can be piped and burned for light and heat. The tar and ammonia are byproducts; sulfur stinks and corrodes. Early gasworks are small; scaling needs chemistry.

name: Gas main and gas network
note: Seamless iron pipe laid underground, distribution on a town or city scale. Requires precision joints, testing for leaks, and reliable supply. Gas is lighter than air: pipes must slope and have drains for condensed tar.

name: Gas meter
note: A wet meter with pistons in a sealed chamber, gas pushing them round, a dial recording revolutions. Charges customers fairly and identifies leaks. Requires careful assembly and sealed joints.

name: Petroleum seeps and collection
note: Oil seeps from rock faces and pools in low ground. Early collection by bucket and pit. No pressure, no depth, just ambient flow. Pitch, naphtha, light oil; use depends on locality.

name: Cable tool drilling (percussion drilling)
note: A steam engine drives a walking beam; a heavy chisel on a cable strikes repeatedly, shattering rock. Bailing removes cuttings and water. Works deep and slow; no rotary motion needed. The first practical oil drilling method.

name: Rotary drilling
note: A spinning drill bit on a hollow rotating rod; drilling mud circulates down the pipe, cooling and carrying cuttings up. Faster, deeper, better for hard rock. Needs precise engineering and circulation pumps.

name: Oil refinery and distillation
note: Crude oil boils at different temperatures; fractional distillation separates light fractions (petrol, kerosene) from heavy (fuel oil, tar). Requires large copper stills, careful heating control, and condensers. The fractions are products, not wastes.

name: Kerosene (paraffin) lamps
note: Kerosene is a clear liquid fraction with a clean flame, brighter than candles or whale oil. Cheaper to refine than to ship coal. Lamps are simple: wick, chimney, brass fitting.

name: Fuel oil (heavy fraction)
note: Heavy oil from the still bottom: too thick to burn in lamps, but a boiler fuel for ships and stationary engines. Higher energy density than coal by weight; viscous, needing heating to flow and atomization to burn.

name: Oil pipeline
note: Welded steel pipe from well to refinery, hundreds of km. Oil is thick; transport by pipeline is cheaper than rail or ship. Requires high pressure seamless pipe, welding skill, and multiple pump stations.

name: Steam turbine (Parsons)
note: Stages of rotor and stator blades; steam expands through each stage, doing work and accelerating. Above a few hundred kW, this beats reciprocating engines: no reciprocating masses, no vibration, compact, efficient. Blade tolerances and metallurgy are severe.

name: Condenser and vacuum
note: A chamber cooled by circulating water, condensing exhaust steam into liquid. This creates a vacuum, pulling the piston back harder, doubling engine power. The cooling water must be copious and clean; copper tubing survives longer than iron.

name: Haystack boiler
note: A rounded iron shell, fire at the bottom, the simplest boiler. Low pressure, small explosion risk, but slow steam generation and poor heat transfer. Used where durability matters more than speed.

name: Wagon boiler
note: Cylindrical shell, internal fire tubes passing through water. More surface area than haystack; faster steam generation. Mobile, used on early locomotives and threshing machines. Prone to scale and tube fouling.

name: Cornish boiler
note: One large fire tube through the water. Rugged, handles high pressure, but prone to violent failure if the tube plugs and overheats. Requires skilled operation and routine inspection.

name: Lancashire boiler
note: Two fire tubes: more heat surface than Cornish, better steam generation. Smaller diameter tubes cool faster if they scale, less dramatic failure. Industrial standard for textile mills and pumping stations.

name: Water-tube boiler
note: Small tubes of water through a chamber of hot gas, boiler in a steel frame. Much higher steam generation than fire-tube types, safer (small volume of water means less explosive stored energy), but more complex assembly and maintenance.

name: Superheating and steam drying
note: Heating saturated steam above boiling point increases its energy density. Dry steam does not corrode pipes and valve seats; water droplets do. Superheaters are pipe coils in the hottest part of the furnace.

name: Feedwater heater and economiser
note: Hot exhaust gas preheats incoming cold water in an economiser; hot condensate is also reused. This cuts fuel consumption significantly. Requires careful design to avoid scale and tube plugging.

name: Safety valve and pressure gauge
note: A weighted spring-loaded valve that lifts at a set pressure, and a Bourdon or liquid gauge to read it. Early boiler explosions killed many; this is the honest lesson that machines need observation and limits. Requires calibration and maintenance.

name: Indicator diagram (Watt's instrument)
note: A small pump coupled to the engine cylinder; a pencil draws a closed curve on a moving drum of paper. The area inside is work; the height is pressure. This turns thermodynamics from guessing into measurement: you can see what the engine actually does.

name: Flywheel and governor
note: The flywheel stores rotary energy, smoothing the lumpy strokes of a reciprocating engine. A centrifugal governor with weighted arms adjusts throttle, keeping speed steady despite changing load. Watt's great innovation.

name: Stirling engine
note: Two cylinders with a hot end and cold end, connected via a regenerator. Displacement and timing are offset so heat is recycled. External combustion, any fuel, but complex mechanics and modest power. Useful for stationary engines where simplicity matters.

name: Gas engine and internal combustion
note: Coal gas is sucked in, mixed with air, sparked, and exploded. Much lighter and simpler than a steam engine. No boiler, no furnace, no engineer. Otto and Diesel engines follow. Early models are unreliable; ignition is the problem.

name: Thermoelectric couple (Seebeck effect)
note: Two different metals joined, one end hot and one cold: a voltage appears. Seebeck discovered this by heating copper-bismuth junctions. Current is tiny but direct: a thermopile of 50 couples can ring a bell.

name: Thermopile as a current source
note: A stack of thermoelectric couples, all hot ends at a furnace, all cold ends at water, producing a steady voltage without zinc consumption. Early telegraph relays and electroplating work used thermopiles before batteries became cheap.

name: Selenium photovoltaic effect
note: Selenium exposed to light generates a voltage. The effect is real but tiny; a palm-sized cell produces microamps. Photo-electric light meters were the first practical use. The efficiency is under 1 percent.

name: Selenium photovoltaic cell
note: A sealed cell with selenium on iron or copper, a back contact and a semi-transparent front. Too fragile and slow for power; used in light meters, exposure control, light-activated switches.

name: Lead-acid storage battery
note: Lead oxide and lead plates in sulfuric acid: charge with DC, discharge to get power. Rechargeable, robust, stores significant energy. The acid eats organic matter and corrodes copper; wood cases and lead terminals are necessary.

name: Nickel-iron battery
note: Nickel oxide and iron electrodes in caustic soda solution. Tougher than lead-acid, tolerates abuse and overcharge, but lower voltage and self-discharge. Edson and Tesla championed it; it is still used in harsh environments.

name: Flywheel energy storage
note: A massive disc or wheel, spun up and allowed to coast. Energy is stored as rotary momentum. Used in pumping stations to store water-mill power and release it on demand, or to smooth reciprocating engine output.

name: Pumped storage hydroelectric
note: Two reservoirs at different elevations: pump water up when power is cheap, run it down to generate when demand is high. Stores energy as gravitational potential; no battery needed. Requires two dams and good geology.

name: High voltage transmission
note: Power loss in a wire is proportional to I squared; raising voltage and lowering current for the same power reduces losses dramatically. Remote hydro becomes economic only with high voltage. Requires transformers, insulators, and careful design.

name: Transformer (step-up/step-down)
note: Two coils on an iron core; AC in one induces AC in the other at a different voltage. No moving parts, highly efficient. Allows voltage conversion without rotating machinery, the key to AC distribution.

name: Three-phase AC and polyphase
note: Three AC waves 120 degrees apart, on three wires. Power delivery is constant instead of pulsing; motors start without a starter and run balanced. Tesla's innovation; it enabled power distribution at scale.

name: Substation and distribution
note: Receives high-voltage transmission lines, steps them down via transformers to local distribution voltage, distributes to neighborhoods and industries. A hub between generation and use; switching and protection equipment required.

name: Load factor and grid economics
note: Load factor is average demand over peak demand. A grid with high load factor is economical: fixed costs (wires, transformers) are spread over more revenue. Time-of-use tariffs and reservoir storage improve load factor.

name: Electric motor and end of line shafting
note: Individual electric motors at each machine, replacing the central steam engine and line shafting running through the factory. This is a larger productivity gain than any single machine: workers control their own pace, maintenance is local, floor space opens up.

name: Fuel cell (hydrogen-oxygen)
note: Hydrogen and oxygen react at separate electrodes in an electrolyte, producing DC directly. Efficient, silent, no heat loss, but hydrogen is expensive to produce. Grove and Schönbein discovered it in the 1840s; Grove built a telegraph powered by fuel cells.

name: Selenium metal extraction
note: Selenium is a trace element in copper ores. Roasting and selective reduction yields grey metallic selenium. The metal is brittle and toxic; handling requires care. Essential for photovoltaic effects.

name: Nuclear fission and power
note: Honest assessment: nuclear power requires uranium enrichment to weapons-grade purity (99.9999+%), neutron physics at a level unknown to Rome, materials research for radiation damage, and a national security programme. The reactor is the easy part. Start this only if you have a state programme with decades and billions to spare.
